title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core challenge in higher education: how to provide timely, meaningful, and scalable formative feedback while preserving pedagogical quality and human oversight. The authors focus on whether teacher, peer, and self-assessments can be reliably combined to support generative AI-based feedback, and they examine the degree of agreement, correlation, and bias across these human evaluative sources. The broader goal is to improve the design of AI-enhanced feedback systems so that they do not treat all human inputs as equally reliable when generating personalized feedback.

The study was conducted within the AICoFe (AI-based Collaborative Feedback) system, which supports rubric-based assessment of students’ oral presentations and is connected to a generative AI model called GePeTo. Students, peers, and the course teacher all used the same validated 15-item rubric covering content, design, and delivery. The empirical analysis used 46 complete evaluation sets and compared teacher rubric scores, two peer evaluations, one self-assessment, and the teacher’s independently assigned overall grade. Statistical analyses examined inter-rater agreement, correlations among evaluator types, and systematic scoring differences.

Participants were 46 final-year undergraduate engineering students in a compulsory oral communication course at Universidad Autonoma de Madrid in Spain. Presentations were delivered individually in a face-to-face classroom setting, with two randomly assigned student peers evaluating each presentation and students later completing self-assessment while reviewing video recordings of their own presentations. The teacher also assessed each presentation using the same rubric and separately assigned an overall grade.

The main conclusions are that teacher, peer, and self-assessments showed moderate to substantial agreement overall, and all evaluator types were positively correlated with the teacher’s overall grade, though teacher rubric scores were most strongly aligned. The study also found systematic bias patterns: peers and self-assessments tended to be slightly more lenient than the teacher’s rubric-based scoring, while the teacher’s own overall grade was somewhat higher than her rubric scores. Based on these findings, the authors propose an enhanced generative AI feedback design that uses weighted integration of evaluator inputs, includes self-assessment, and explicitly detects bias and divergence before generating context-aware feedback.

identified_tools.name: AICoFe
identified_tools.description: AICoFe (AI-based Collaborative Feedback / Artificial Intelligence-based Collaborative Feedback System) is a named system that integrates teacher, peer, and self-assessments using a rubric and a generative AI component to produce personalized feedback for students.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper analyzed 46 evaluation sets within AICoFe for engineering students’ oral presentations to examine agreement, correlation, and bias across teacher, peer, and self-assessments, with results used to propose an enhanced GenAI feedback design.

findings.finding_summary: Across 46 full evaluation sets, inter-rater agreement in AICoFe was moderate to substantial by Gwet’s AC2 but weak by weighted Cohen’s kappa. Pairwise agreement ranged from κw=0.22 to 0.30 and AC2=0.58 to 0.63; overall concordance was Kendall’s W=0.51 for teacher and peers and 0.46 when including self-assessments, with global AC2=0.66 in both cases.
findings.measure: Inter-rater agreement on rubric-based oral presentation scores (weighted Cohen’s kappa, Gwet’s AC2, Kendall’s W, exact agreement)

findings.finding_summary: Rubric-based scores within AICoFe were significantly correlated with the teacher’s independently assigned overall grade. The strongest correlation was for the teacher rubric mean (Pearson’s r=0.88; Spearman’s ρ=0.89), followed by the mean across all evaluators (r=0.85; ρ=0.86), peers rubric mean (r=0.69; ρ=0.68), and self-assessment rubric mean (r=0.59; ρ=0.67); all p<0.001.
findings.measure: Correlation between rubric-based scores and teacher’s overall grade for oral presentations

findings.finding_summary: Bias analyses in AICoFe showed systematic score differences across evaluators. Teacher rubric scores were significantly lower than peers (mean difference=-0.49, p=0.008) and lower than the teacher’s own overall grade (mean difference=-0.37, p<0.001), while self-assessments were significantly higher than teacher rubric scores (mean difference=+0.36, p=0.037); comparisons between self and peers and between self and teacher overall grade were not significant.
findings.measure: Mean differences in rubric/grade scores across teacher, peer, and self-assessment sources

identified_tools.name: GePeTo
identified_tools.description: GePeTo is a generative AI-based personalized guidance and feedback model integrated into educational dashboards/systems to generate customized feedback from assessment and analytics inputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Within AICoFe, GePeTo was the generative model used to produce personalized feedback from rubric-based teacher and peer assessments; this paper did not empirically test a new GePeTo version but proposed enhancements including weighted input aggregation, bias detection, and context-aware feedback generation.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical single-study analysis using correlational and agreement statistics on 46 evaluation sets, not an RCT or quasi-experimental design. It provides useful evidence about reliability and bias patterns but does not causally estimate learning effects of the AI system.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports associations and agreement metrics rather than intervention effect sizes on student learning outcomes. Findings suggest promising alignment and identifiable bias patterns, but impact on learning or feedback quality remains unclear and is proposed for future validation.
